name: secure-proxy
intent: Interpose a chain of security gates in which each gate authenticates and authorises the request on its own evidence before passing it inward, so that nesting one protected system inside another satisfies both policies and no gate has to trust another gate's verdict.
problem: Two enforcement points guard the same resources - a reverse proxy in front of an application, an API gateway in front of a service and its sidecar, an outer system whose enclave contains an inner one - and the request must satisfy both policies. Both naive resolutions fail: let the inner gate trust the outer one and a single mistake, misconfiguration or bypass silently opens the resource; make the subject satisfy both gates naively and it either repeats the authentication dialog at every layer or has to disclose its credentials to the first gate, which can then impersonate it.
context: Composition of protected systems across a trust boundary: an application behind an edge proxy or API gateway, a service behind a sidecar or service mesh, an outer system that encapsulates an inner security domain, or a chain of filters, middleware, interceptors or layers inside one process. It applies where different parties own the two policies, where every path into the inner resources crosses the inner gate, and where the subject's identity has to be re-established or delegated at the inner boundary without disclosing secrets or handing the outer gate the subject's rights.
benefits: Both policies are enforced instead of merged: the outer and inner requirements are each satisfied where they are owned, so an inner system's rules do not have to be expressed in the outer system's language or disclosed to the outer owner.

Independent checking is what turns a stack of layers into defence in depth: each gate decides from its own evidence and its own policy, so a bug, a misconfiguration or a compromised layer does not by itself grant access to the resources behind the next gate.

Each gate stays small, locally owned and separately testable: the outer gate's tests cover admission to the enclave and the inner gate's tests cover its own resources, without a combined policy that neither team can review.

The subject can sign on once when a delegation scheme is chosen, instead of repeating the full authentication dialog at every gate - and its long-term credential need not be disclosed to the outer gate at all in the trusted-proxy and identity-asserting forms.

Which relationship the two gates use becomes an explicit design decision with a recorded tradeoff (password disclosure, impersonation risk, single sign-on, delegation-protocol support) instead of an accident of whoever wrote the first proxy.
Gates can be added, removed or reordered without editing the protected code, because each one is a separate wrapper around the same request path and each owns a single concern.
tradeoffs: No relationship between the gates is ideal: every choice trades usability (single sign-on), disclosure risk (the subject's password or long-term credential reaching the outer gate), impersonation risk (the outer gate acting for the subject at the inner gate) and deployment cost (a delegation protocol both ends must implement).

Every nested gate sits on the request path: a login tunnel re-authenticates the subject at the inner boundary, and any gate that verifies a signed assertion or certificate chain pays signature, trust-anchor and revocation cost on every request.

Identity propagation is the failure-prone part: an inner gate that accepts an identity the outer gate merely asserts - a header, a claim, a source address, a certificate name it did not validate - degenerates into a rubber stamp and creates a confused deputy, and the trust relationship between the gates then has to be authenticated too.

Authorising the outer gate instead of the subject leaks that gate's broader rights to everything it forwards, so one compromised or over-privileged component grants its privileges to every caller behind it.

More keys, certificates, trust anchors, error mappings and logs to operate, and a layered denial is hard to attribute without a per-gate audit trail; failures can be misdiagnosed as belonging to the wrong layer.

Delegations and assertions need bounded lifetimes and a revocation story, because a credential cached by the outer gate for a later login is standing impersonation risk, and re-validating on every request trades that risk against latency.
Nesting two gates that implement the same check with the same evidence adds cost and operational surface without adding depth; independent layers must be able to fail independently.

participants.responsibility: The user, service or process requesting a protected resource; it authenticates to the outer gate and may hold a credential or delegation that the inner gate can verify for itself.

First enforcement point at the outer boundary: authenticates the subject, enforces the outer policy, and forwards the request inward under an explicitly chosen identity - its own, the subject's credentials, or a delegation scoped to the subject.

Second enforcement point inside the nested system: authenticates and authorises the request independently, from its own policy and evidence, and never treats the existence of the outer gate as proof of identity or authority.
A boundary that owns one gate and the resources behind it; nesting two enclaves is the structure that creates the problem, and each enclave keeps its own policy, keys and audit trail.

The artifact that carries verified subject identity across the inner boundary - a signed token, ticket or certificate chain - accepted by the inner gate only when issuer, audience, scope and lifetime validate.
The rules each gate consults, owned locally by that enclave's authority so that neither gate has to interpret or trust the other's policy.

use_cases: TLS-terminating reverse proxy or API gateway in front of an application or a service-mesh sidecar: the gateway authenticates the client, and the service (or its sidecar) validates the token or client certificate again against the issuer's keys instead of trusting an identity header the gateway happened to set.

Enterprise single sign-on with delegation or token exchange: a portal authenticates the user once and calls back-end services with a token scoped to the user and the transaction (Kerberos constrained delegation, OAuth token exchange, a SAML bearer assertion), so each service authorises the user rather than the portal.

Layered enclaves in a high-assurance or multi-level system: an inner enclave's guard enforces its own policy on top of the outer system's, with the outer guard acting under its own identity or under an identity-asserting protocol the inner guard trusts.

In-process request pipelines: servlet filters, ASP.NET Core middleware, Rack-style middleware stacks, Django's onion middleware, Ktor plugins or tower layers, where authentication, request validation and authorisation gates run in a defined order and each can short-circuit the rest.

Kernel-level gate stacks: seccomp filter trees, where further filters may be added and each filter in the tree is evaluated in order and can only narrow what the earlier ones allow, and interposed shared libraries (loader preloading, audit modules) that each constrain what reaches the resource.

Multi-tenant or partner-facing platforms where the outer gate enforces the contract (plan, rate limits, routing, tenant selection) and the inner service independently enforces per-tenant authorisation over its own data.

Istio/Envoy end-user authentication: a RequestAuthentication policy at the ingress gateway validates the request JWT against the issuer's JWKS, and a same-or-narrower-scoped policy in front of the workload makes each sidecar re-validate the token for itself; claim-based routing then reads metadata derived from the validated JWT rather than from any client-supplied header.

oauth2-proxy in front of an application: the proxy authenticates the browser at the edge and hands the upstream signed evidence instead of a bare assertion - HMAC-signed identity headers (GAP-Signature via --signature-key) or an access token the upstream can verify - because the project's own advisories show unsigned identity headers being defeated by header spoofing and header smuggling.

Envoy's jwt_authn filter as a gate that owns its evidence: it verifies signature, issuer, audiences and exp/nbf against locally configured or remotely fetched JWKS, rejects the request on failure, and forwards the verified payload upstream only where claim_to_headers or forward is explicitly configured - verified identity is an explicit artifact, never an implicit assumption.
avoid_when: There is one trust domain and one policy: a single Protected System with one guard (Policy + Guard) is simpler and just as strong; nesting gates that share owner, evidence and rules buys hops, not security.

The inner gate cannot verify anything for itself - if all it can do is trust an unauthenticated header or an assumed network position, use one enforcement point at the outermost boundary (see Reference Monitor) until identity can be propagated verifiably, rather than shipping a gate that cannot say no.
The path is latency-critical and both gates belong to one owner and one policy: one gate plus complete mediation at the boundary is cheaper than two gates checking the same thing.

The platform already nests enforcement with verified identity (service mesh mutual TLS with workload identities and policy engines at both ends, or a cloud load balancer with authenticated origin pulls): configure it rather than rebuilding the gates in application code.

A second path into the inner resources exists - an admin network, direct storage access, a debug endpoint, a second listener: fix the mediation so one unbypassable gate covers every path before adding another layer, because a bypassable chain is not defence in depth.
anti_patterns: "Authorizing proxy" drift: the outer gate authorises and the inner gate is configured to let everything from it through (or exempts its address), so the inner policy exists only on paper and the outer gate's privileges become every caller's privileges.

Trusting an unverified caller identity: an inner service reads a user header, token claim or client-certificate name without validating issuer, audience and signature - the classic header-spoofing and confused-deputy hole in proxy chains.
Duplicate layers presented as defence in depth: the same check copied into two gates shares the same bugs and adds latency and operational surface rather than depth.
A gate that never denies: a failed check falls through (fail open), an exception in the check is treated as success, or the gate logs "authenticated" and forwards anyway.

Optional mediation: the inner resources remain reachable through an admin route, debug endpoint, second listener or direct storage access, so crossing the chain of gates is a choice rather than a requirement.
design_principles: Defence in depth: independent, non-identical layers, so that the failure of one gate is not the failure of the protection.
Complete mediation within each enclave: every path from outside crosses the outer gate and every path into the inner resources crosses the inner gate.
Fail-safe defaults: a gate that cannot verify identity, evidence or policy denies the request.
Separation of concerns and local policy ownership: each gate enforces the policy of the resources it guards, and the two policies stay in different hands.
Least privilege and least disclosure: each gate sees only what it needs - never the subject's long-term secret - and delegations grant the minimum scope and lifetime.
Economy of mechanism: each gate stays small enough to review and test on its own, because it is the component an attacker studies first.
best_practices: Make each gate independently enforceable: it must verify identity and authority from evidence it can validate itself and deny on its own, treating any upstream verdict as a hint rather than a permission.

Authenticate the channel and the assertion between the gates (mutual TLS, signed tokens, a shared trust anchor), validate issuer, audience, scope and expiry at the inner gate, and treat key rotation and trust-store updates as first-class operations.

Choose the relationship between the gates deliberately - trusted proxy, authenticating or identity-asserting impersonation, delegation, login tunnel - and record which tradeoff it makes between password disclosure, impersonation risk, single sign-on and protocol support.

Prefer a delegation scoped to the user and the transaction over the outer gate's own identity; where the outer gate must act as itself, give it a narrow principal of its own and audit what it does with it.
Bound delegations and assertions in time, scope and audience, and re-validate on each request rather than caching a verified identity for the life of a connection.
Log allow and deny decisions at every gate together with the gate's identity, so a layered denial is attributable and a gate that never denies becomes visible.
Keep gate order declarative (pipeline configuration, filter registration) and versioned, because the effective policy depends on the order and on which gates are enabled.
Test the layering: each gate alone must reject what it should, and a simulated failure or bypass of one gate must leave the remaining gates enforcing.
sources: The Open Group, Technical Guide: Security Design Patterns (Blakley, Heath and members of the Open Group Security Forum, April 2004, Doc. No. G031) - Section 8.8 Secure Proxy (pp. 79-85): the relationship between the guards of two nested Protected System instances, its six variants (Trusted Proxy, Authenticating Impersonator, Identity-Asserting Impersonator, Delegate, Authorizing Proxy, Login Tunnel) and the consequences table of password disclosure, impersonation risk, single sign-on and delegation-protocol support.

NIST Special Publication 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture (Rose, Borchert, Mitchell & Connelly, August 2020) - no implicit trust is granted to assets or accounts based on network location, and authentication and authorisation are discrete functions evaluated at the enforcement point before a resource is reached; the principle behind requiring every gate in a chain to check for itself.

Romanowsky, Security Design Patterns Part 1 (Morgan Stanley Online, September 2001) - the "Layered Security" pattern cited in [TG_SDP] section 8.8 as a known use of stacking independent protection layers.

Kienzle, Elder, Tyree & Edwards-Hewitt, Security Patterns Repository, Version 1.0 - the "Trusted Proxy" pattern cited in [TG_SDP] section 8.8 Known Uses, the realisation in which the outer guard forwards under its own identity.
